articles.title: A calmer interface starts with fewer decisions
articles.html:
A minimal interface makes the next step easy to identify. Removing elements helps only when the remaining controls still explain what someone can do.

Choose what deserves attention

On an article page, reading is the main activity. The title introduces the subject, the body develops it, and navigation helps someone return to the feed. Sharing and comments should remain available without competing with the text.

Use space with intention

Keep related information close together. Use larger gaps when the purpose changes, such as between an article and its comments. Check the result on a phone and a desktop: equal spacing does not always look balanced at both sizes.

Keep the quiet details useful

Reserve space for images before they load. Make keyboard focus visible. When someone returns from an article, restore their filters and scroll position. These details make the interface predictable without adding more controls.
articles.excerpt: Clear hierarchy, useful spacing, and predictable navigation.

articles.title: Build one useful feature at a time
articles.html:
A useful feature starts with a specific task. Before opening the editor, I write down what someone should be able to do when the work is finished. If that requires several unrelated steps, I reduce the scope.

Start with one clear outcome

For a personal finance tool, the first task could be recording an expense. The initial version needs an amount, a date, and a way to save. Dashboards and predictions can wait until that basic flow works.

Make the feedback visible

After saving, the interface should confirm what happened. Show the new entry and a short confirmation. If saving fails, keep the information already entered and explain how to retry.

Leave room for the next iteration

Once the basic flow works, review where someone hesitates. Add the next feature when it solves a specific problem. Keep each change small enough to test independently.
articles.excerpt: A simple expense flow: enter, save, and confirm.

articles.title: Test Post #1 update
articles.html:
I’m currently building my website and working on connecting Substack as a secondary blogging platform. I want to bring the content I publish on Substack into my website so readers can see it there and, if they want, continue reading on Substack.

At the start.


For the initial release of this second version of my website, I’ll pull posts from Substack. In the future, my idea is to display the content directly on my website and create a dedicated page for each article.

I’m currently reviewing the documentation to understand how to connect Substack to an external website. I find this interesting because it’s similar to integrations I’ve already worked on, such as connecting Google Calendar and using EmailJS to send information and emails.
